name: Dusky Rose
lede: Dusky Rose is a muted, slightly brownish pink, built by putting the modifier dusky in front of the base color rose rather than naming anything in particular.

sections.title: A modifier on rose
sections.body:
Dusky Rose puts the modifier word dusky in front of the base color [[rose]], in the compound-modifier grammar ColorHub's library uses for descriptive names like this one [1]. The name entered the xkcd color survey of 2010, where volunteers labeled a swatch grid with whatever words they chose, rather than any older dictionary or standard [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[dusty-rose]], only 3.5 units off, close enough on screen to read as the same pink [1]; [[mayflower]] sits 4.8 units off, and [[antique-rose]] 5.5 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within six units of this swatch in only 34 of 23,781 paintings, 0.14 percent, as photographed; looking inside each painting for at least five percent coverage narrows that to 11 [2]. That makes it rarer than 67 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 55 percent of its 11 appearances by lightness rank [2].

The earliest match dates to the year 1000, a thousand years before the name's 2010 record, so it marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment or dye [2]. In printed English the word rose fastest in the 1920s, well before the name reached xkcd's volunteers, a reminder that a search for "dusky rose" in that era is catching the flower and the general phrase, not yet this specific color [2].
